does: Cooks food uncovered in the dry heat of a hot oven, so that the outside browns while the inside cooks in its own juices.

intro.what: Roasting uses the dry heat of an oven to brown food in an uncovered tin.
intro.why: It connects surface dryness and space in the tin with browning and the juices left for a sauce.

how: Dry the surface of the food well.
Season it, and rub it with a little fat.
Set it in a tin that fits it without crowding, in an oven that is fully hot.
Turn it or baste it now and then, so that it browns evenly.
Rest it before carving, and make a jus from what is left in the tin.

cues.text: A deep golden-brown surface, and browned juices stuck to the tin.
A rich roasting smell fills the kitchen well before the food is done.
A steady sizzle from the tin.

mistakes.mistake: Crowding the tin, so that the food steams and stays pale.
mistakes.fix: Leave space around every piece, or use a second tin.

mistakes.mistake: Carving a roast straight from the oven.

quiz.question: What does the uncovered dry heat of roasting help develop?
quiz.because: Uncovered dry oven heat browns the outside of the food.

quiz.question: What do you do to the surface before seasoning and adding fat?
choices: Soak the surface and leave it wet.
Wrap the food tightly in foil.
quiz.because: Start with a dry surface before seasoning and adding a little fat.

quiz.question: Which appearance matches the browning described here?
choices: A pale surface in pooled water.
A wet, pale surface with little colour in the tin.
A golden-brown surface and browned juices in the tin.
quiz.because: A golden-brown surface and browned juices in the tin show the browning this method develops.

quiz.question: Food in a crowded tin is steaming and staying pale. What would you change?
choices: Leave room around the pieces or use another tin.
Pack more food into the same tin.
Cover the tin tightly to trap steam.
quiz.because: Crowded pieces steam and stay pale. More space, or another tin, gives them room to brown.

comes_after.why: Roasting is searing done by an oven: the same dry surface and the same patience, on a larger piece.
